own_scenes.desc: El imperio de Kenny Gamble y Leon Huff, distribuido por CBS: los O’Jays, los Intruders, Billy Paul y Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes con Teddy Pendergrass, sobre la banda de la casa MFSB (Norman Harris, Bobby Eli, Ronnie Baker, Earl Young), la más exitosa de los setenta; su «TSOP» fue la sintonía de Soul Train. Los O’Jays fueron el altavoz del comentario social de Gamble: «Back Stabbers» (1972), Ship Ahoy (1974) con su travesía en un barco negrero, «For the Love of Money» (que el éxito convirtió en música de centro comercial), Survival, Family Reunion. Después de 1976 desapareció el mensaje del soul, y con Gloria Gaynor y Donna Summer la frontera entre el disco, el funk y el soul se borró.

refs.q: But for seventies soul strength, the Philadelphia International empire, led by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, were the leaders of the pack.
refs.para: But for seventies soul strength, the Philadelphia International empire, led by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, were the leaders of the pack. Hooked up with and distributed by CBS Records, the Philly Sound boasted a lineup that included the O’Jays, the Intruders, Billy Paul, and Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes featuring Theodore Pendergrass, as well as the house band, MFSB (Mother, Father, Sister, Brother). Every one of these acts scored huge national hits and brought a down-home vocal style into Gamble and Huff’s candy-coated string ensemble arrangements.

refs.q: The message in soul music all but disappeared.
refs.para: The O’Jays were a magnificent singing group that could handle the hottest funk tracks while blending smooth harmonies and tender ballads with social statements. But like most of the soul singers, after 1976 there was no longer a message in the music, and unlike Aretha Franklin’s symbolic “Respect,” there was no longer any mandate from black America to be made by middle-class—oriented soul artists. The message in soul music all but disappeared.

podcast.title: Characteristics
podcast.body: The Philly Sound, exemplified by The Spinners working with producer Thom Bell, is characterized by a distinctive combination of "gorgeous falsetto, the lush orchestration, the smoothly polished sound." "That the gorgeous falsetto, the lush orchestration, the smoothly polished sound, it's all evident here in one of a kind love affair."

podcast.title: Distinct R&B Style
podcast.body: The Philly Sound is identified as a distinct style within R&B, characterized by its smooth, orchestral arrangements. First Choice's "Armed and Extremely Dangerous" is described as being "very much in the Philly Sound vein," indicating its musical characteristics. "It's a good song, very much in the Philly Sound vein, and it made it to number 11 on the R&B chart, but not a pop hit."
